title: How the Iran War Spiked Oil Prices
summary: Explainer on why the 2026 Hormuz closure cut global oil supply only about 8 percent yet spiked prices 60 percent: inelastic demand, bypass pipelines, trader sentiment, war-risk insurance, and a lasting risk premium.

assertions.quote: Prices, however, spiked a massive 60%, seven and a half times more than the contraction in supply.

verdicts.note: The Hormuz closure cut global supply and sent crude toward 100 dollars a barrel; US pump prices rose by more than a dollar a gallon in the following weeks.

assertions.quote: So, why does an 8% contraction in supply lead to a 60% jump in price?

verdicts.note: Estimates of short-run oil demand elasticity cluster near -0.1, so a supply cut of a few percent implies a price move of tens of percent.

assertions.quote: Collectively, these four pipelines provide considerable export capacity, dampening the impact of the strait's closure.

verdicts.note: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline (about 5 million barrels a day to Yanbu) and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah line can carry a large share of Gulf exports around the strait.

assertions.quote: the day-to-day movements follow a mix of narrative and reality.

verdicts.note: Oil futures price expected supply, so prices jump on announcements and shift on sentiment before physical flows change.

In a calibrated model of geopolitical oil-supply risk, a rise in the probability of a production disaster raises the oil price through precautionary inventory demand even when no disaster occurs (about 4% for a 10pp shock to 9% for a 40pp shock), consistent with the 1979 and 1990 episodes; a model result, not a direct test of trader behaviour.

assertions.quote: Regardless of the physical impediments, bureaucratic ones made it functionally impossible for oil to flow out of the Gulf.

verdicts.note: Tankers cannot sail uninsured, and Joint War Committee listings with 72-hour cancellation have stopped traffic in the Red Sea and Black Sea in recent years.

assertions.quote: The market will likely price this uncertainty in long-term.

verdicts.note: A prediction; risk premia faded within months after the 1991 Gulf War and the 2019 Abqaiq attack, but a demonstrated closure is a larger shock.

The paper shows markets price the probability of a Gulf supply disruption (the June 2025 Iran-Israel war lifted the Hormuz-closure probability 13 points and the oil price 9%), but it calls that rise temporary and models the premium as fading with the probability, so it supports the risk-pricing mechanism without showing that prices stay above pre-war levels once a conflict ends.
